references.text: Blue, purple, and scarlet yarn are used in the making of tabernacle curtains, the same materials mentioned in 25:4
The curtain for the Most Holy Place was to be made of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen
The curtain for the tent entrance was to be made from the same colored materials
The gate to the courtyard was to have a curtain of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen
The priestly garments, including the ephod, were to be made of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen
The breastpiece was to be made from the same materials as the ephod
Repetition of the gifts that were to be gathered, including blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, fine linen, and goat hair
The people brought the mentioned materials as offerings for the tabernacle
Skilled women spun blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, as well as goat hair
The holy garments were made of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn
Blue, purple, and scarlet coverings are used to cover sacred objects during transport
Solomon requests craftsmen who can work with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn for the temple construction
The curtain in the temple was made of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen
The same holy colors and textiles from the tabernacle's construction (25:4) are used to equip the priest's service in 28:5.
The instruction about materials in 25:4 is specified as the skilled making of the priest's ephod in 28:6.
The making of the ephod in 39:2 confirms that the materials and instructions from 25:4 were followed exactly.
The making of the entrance curtain in 36:37 shows that the materials from 25:4 were used consistently throughout the construction of the tabernacle.
The holy colors from 25:4 are also used for the priest's sash (39:29), which emphasizes the unity of the holy service.
The materials from 25:4 are handled by the God-given craftsmen (38:23), showing that both material and human gifts are necessary for God's house.
